content:
Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses and the newer cheaper non-designer models all come with AI features, but in early July, the company announced a "ridiculous" cap on free uses of an accessibility feature.

In effect, Meta has retroactively placed a paywall on a hardware product already sold to customers. Update: the social network now says it will "pause" its paywall plans for this feature — see the end of the article.

Meta first began rolling out Conversation Focus last December.

This is one of those clever uses of AI where one of the big advantages is on-device processing, which neither compromises privacy nor uses mobile data.

However, The Verge reports that Meta is now setting a cap on free uses of the feature.

This is especially unacceptable. First, as the site's reporter Sean Hollister notes, the feature runs on-device, without using Meta's servers, so there is no reason at all to charge users for it. Second, this is an accessibility feature, and some users may have bought the glasses precisely for this feature.

When The Verge asked Meta about it, the company replied that the limit "currently" applies only to Conversation Focus, implying that other AI features may also have usage caps in the future. Meta tells us that because the feature is designed for people with normal hearing, it does not consider it an accessibility feature. I think that's just playing with words, because in noisy environments, some people genuinely have a harder time following conversations.

All of this may be good news for the upcoming Apple Glasses — it gives consumers yet another reason to buy their AI smart glasses from a company with a better reputation, even at a higher upfront cost. Apple has always emphasized that it never seeks a return on investment for accessibility features, instead seeing them as a contribution to a better world.

Apple Glasses are expected to launch sometime next year.

Update: Meta told The Verge that it has paused plans to limit users' use of Conversation Focus, but has not given up the idea of putting paywalls on some of the glasses' features.
